**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date to the Appointment tab. It shows how ready the MenoMap notes are and what would make them stronger.
- Pick the most important topics and questions. Limit it to three or four.
- Create notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check whether your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: the numbers, averages, heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

The notes are a summary of the information you entered and the data you chose to add from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record; the patterns in them are also a coincidence check, not proof of cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer; that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add new medications with their start dates. After a few weeks MenoMap can show your records from before and after; this makes the next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day the 12th consecutive month without a period is completed, not explained by another cause (pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s; but it is also common at any time from the mid-40s to the mid-50s.

**Perimenopause** is the years leading up to this point. Hormone levels rise and fall irregularly; so periods may become irregular, heavier or lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin in this period, while periods are still continuing. Perimenopause can last a few years or much longer and goes differently for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is the whole period after this 12-month threshold. Some symptoms fade over time; some can last for years.

Menopause can also happen earlier, due to surgery removing the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other health problems. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called early ovarian failure (premature ovarian failure) and is worth talking to a doctor about.

**How is it recognised?** In many people over 45, doctors recognise perimenopause or menopause from history and symptoms. Because hormone levels change from day to day, blood tests are not always needed. Blood tests are used more when the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What does MenoMap do and not do?** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment. So you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat usually felt in the face, neck and chest; sometimes accompanied by flushing, sweating, a fast heartbeat or chills afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep and can be strong enough to wake you or soak your sheets.

They are among the most common changes of the menopause period. Some people have a few mild hot flashes; others have many a day, disrupting work and sleep. In some they fade within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** People often notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or a heavy duvet. These vary greatly from person to person; so tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Flushing and sweating can also come from thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms don't fit the usual pattern or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell a doctor.

**Describing them well.** Useful details for the appointment:
- Roughly how many there are by day and night
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What happened before
- What you tried and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Wave button and after-the-fact logging exist to record exactly this without much effort.

**Help is possible.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options and practical approaches. Which suit you is something to discuss with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen the body makes less of during menopause. Leading guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people; it may help other symptoms too.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. People who have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen along with estrogen to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks vary by person:** age, time since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and the type and route of treatment. So this is not a decision an app can give, but one to make together with a doctor who knows your history.

**Common questions:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, why or why not?
- Which type and form would you recommend, why?
- Which benefits can I expect, and how soon?
- What are my personal risks and how do they compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for and when should we reassess this?

**If you already use it,** record it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap shows your waves before and after starting as a coincidence check, not as proof; so you have something concrete to talk about at the review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not right for everyone and some people prefer other routes. There are several options.

**Prescription options.** There is evidence that some non-hormonal medications reduce hot flashes. These include some medications actually developed for other conditions and a newer class designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions; a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapies and mind-body approaches.** There is evidence that cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to menopause makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes people find helpful:**
- Layers you can remove quickly
- A fan at your desk and next to your bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here)
- Regular movement and a regular sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal products.** For many the evidence is conflicting or limited, quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist everything you use, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own records before a change and during it; this is easier to assess than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. People usually remember the latest days or the worst days. A simple record fills this gap.

**What a symptom diary gives your doctor:**
- Not only that symptoms happen, but how often and how strong
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only works if you keep it. MenoMap is built on a one-tap Wave button and a four-question evening check-in; so it takes a few seconds, not a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down the ones most important to you: the symptom bothering you most, things you want to try or avoid and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Appointment tab helps you choose questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
After 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**; even if it happened only once and even if it is only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Often the cause turns out not to be serious. For example, thinning of the vagina or uterine lining is common. But postmenopausal bleeding can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. That is why public health guidance says to have it checked rather than wait.

**If you use hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns may be expected depending on the type you use. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or at the wrong time should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or health service and say you have postmenopausal bleeding.
- Note the date, amount and anything else you notice. MenoMap can keep this for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It reminds you to have it checked and adds the bleeding to your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints of midlife and rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly or leave you too hot or damp to fall back asleep.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but tends to disrupt the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or your partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing; these can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth discussing especially if you are very sleepy in the daytime)

**What usually helps people.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers you can remove; a fixed wake-up time and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-researched approach; many doctors can refer you to it.

**What to track.** For a week or two note your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check-in and Wave log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside night sweats as context, not as an explanation.

**When to get it checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example while driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night.
